title: The Valedictory I Never Gave
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] They asked me to say a few words at my own retirement dinner, and I declined, ostensibly out of modesty, though the truer reason was that thirty-one years resist compression into anything a room full of colleagues could politely applaud between courses.
Narrator: So here, instead, is the valedictory I withheld, addressed to no audience but the ceiling of my study and whatever remains of my vanity.

Narrator: [carefully] I did not become a better teacher by accumulating certainty, as the brochures would have you believe; I became one by relinquishing it, semester by grudging semester, until I could stand before a lecture hall and confess ignorance without flinching.

Narrator: The students who unsettled me most were never the indifferent ones but the earnest ones, the sort who took my offhand remarks as doctrine and quoted them back to me years later with a reverence I hadn't earned and privately found alarming.

Narrator: [reflective] I used to believe my discipline was in decline, that each incoming cohort read less carefully than the last, and I have since concluded this was less an observation than an occupational vanity, the comforting delusion that one's own generation marked some high-water mark of seriousness.
Narrator: Every generation of professors, I suspect, mistakes its own fading stamina for the world's decline.

Narrator: [honestly] What I will actually miss is unglamorous: the particular hush before a seminar turns, the moment a mediocre argument suddenly reorganizes itself into something rigorous under gentle interrogation.

Narrator: I never once cured a student of laziness through eloquence alone; the ones who changed did so quietly, on their own schedule, usually for reasons that had nothing to do with anything I'd said.
Narrator: [gently] Vanity again, perhaps, but I'd like to think I occasionally supplied the pretext under which that private transformation felt permissible.

Narrator: So, no valedictory, no applause between courses. Only this: teaching was never the noble transmission of certainty I'd imagined at twenty-five. It was the slower, humbler art of admitting what I did not know, convincingly enough that someone else felt safe admitting it too.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator decline to give a speech at her retirement dinner?
options: Thirty-one years resisted compression into something suitable for polite applause between courses
She had nothing to say
She was too emotional to speak
The event organizers forgot to invite her
quiz.explanation: She says the truer reason was that thirty-one years resist compression into anything a room could politely applaud between courses.

quiz.question: According to the narrator, how did she become a better teacher?
options: By accumulating certainty over time
By relinquishing certainty, semester by grudging semester
By memorizing more material
By avoiding difficult questions
quiz.explanation: She says she became a better teacher by relinquishing certainty, not accumulating it.

quiz.question: Which students unsettled the narrator most?
options: The indifferent ones
Students who never attended class
The earnest ones who quoted her offhand remarks back as doctrine
Students who challenged her openly
quiz.explanation: She says the earnest students who treated her remarks as doctrine unsettled her most.

quiz.question: What conclusion does she reach about believing her discipline was in decline?
options: It was an accurate observation
It was confirmed by data
It only applied to certain students
It was likely an occupational vanity, mistaking her own fading stamina for the world's decline
quiz.explanation: She concludes every generation of professors mistakes its own fading stamina for the world's decline.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude teaching actually was?
options: The humbler art of admitting what she did not know, convincingly enough for others to do the same
The noble transmission of certainty
A purely administrative task
A way to gain prestige
quiz.explanation: She concludes teaching was the humbler art of admitting ignorance convincingly enough that students felt safe doing the same.

quiz.question: What central claim does “The Valedictory I Never Gave” develop?
options: Assessment can reward compliance more reliably than understanding.
A teacher’s legacy resists a neat public summary.
Unfinished work can record genuine intellectual apprenticeship.
Perfectionism can become a strategy for avoiding completion.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports the reasoning in “The Valedictory I Never Gave”?
options: Rigid assessment may favour students with existing cultural capital.
Abandoning a premise can show thought has developed.
Relinquishing certainty models intellectual honesty.
Repeated revisions shift toward increasingly trivial concerns.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which qualification prevents an oversimplified reading of “The Valedictory I Never Gave”?
options: Structure can protect students who cannot easily demand it.
Mastery does not always progress in a straight line.
Public work requires choosing which flaws can remain.
Changing stamina does not prove that learning has declined.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which response best expresses the speaker’s stance in “The Valedictory I Never Gave”?
options: The narrator values admitting ignorance publicly.
The speaker distinguishes rigorous thinking from efficient throughput.
The narrator treats the drawer as an honest record of revision.
The apprentice is urged to finish rather than endlessly refine.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: What implication follows most clearly from “The Valedictory I Never Gave”?
options: A fair exam system must examine what its form rewards.
Education benefits when authority makes room for uncertainty.
Learning includes leaving convictions behind for sound reasons.
Standards matter, but completion exposes work to real learning.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.
